_method: primary sources fetched live (gov.ie, citizensinformation.ie, workplacerelations.ie); verbatim quotes in source.quote; 2027 NMW, post-Oct-2026 PRSI steps, sick-leave increases and Tips Act amendments checked and excluded as unannounced/unverified

entries.title: Irish National Minimum Wage rose to €14.15 on 1 January 2026
entries.fact: The Republic of Ireland national minimum wage increased by 65 cents, from €13.50 to €14.15 per hour, on 1 January 2026.

quantification.how: €0.65/hr increase × 39h × 52wk = €1,318.20 per full-time minimum-wage employee per year (wage cost only, before employer PRSI on the increase)

source.quote: The national minimum wage increased by 65 cents to €14.15 per hour on 1 January 2026.

entries.angle: Since 1 January the Irish minimum wage has been €14.15 — roughly €1,300 more per full-time hourly employee per year than 2025. For a multi-site group, that lands as a five-figure labour-line increase per venue estate this year.
entries.proof_pairing: Customer proof showing labour cost as % of revenue brought down or held flat through better scheduling/forecasting accuracy (e.g. a multi-site IE/UK operator case with a quantified labour % reduction).
entries.caveats: Applies to workers aged 20 and over; sub-minimum youth rates are €12.74 (19), €11.32 (18), €9.91 (under 18) per the same source family (citizensinformation.ie minimum wage page, fetched 2026-08-20). Arithmetic assumes a 39-hour week; actual hours vary. Only bites directly on staff at or near the minimum; many hospitality roles pay above it. Budget 2027 (October 2026) sets the next step — re-verify after Budget day.

entries.title: Employer PRSI Class A rates currently 9% / 11.25%
entries.fact: Employers in Ireland currently pay Class A employer PRSI of 9% on weekly earnings up to €552 and 11.25% on weekly earnings above €552 (rates in force until 30 September 2026).

source.quote: On 1 January 2026, the weekly earnings threshold increased and employers pay: 9% Class A employer PRSI on weekly earnings up to €552 11.25% Class A employer PRSI if weekly earnings are above €552

entries.angle: Best used as the baseline fact inside an email about the 1 October 2026 step-up: every payroll euro in an Irish venue already carries 11.25% employer PRSI on full-time hospitality wages, and that rate rises again on 1 October 2026.
entries.proof_pairing: Payroll-accuracy / labour-forecasting proof: a customer story where payroll processing errors or unplanned overtime (each euro of which carries employer PRSI) was reduced measurably.
entries.caveats: This is the current rate level, not a new increase in itself — the last 0.1 percentage-point step took effect 1 October 2025 and the €552 threshold changed 1 January 2026. Confirmed against the gov.ie PRSI Class A rates table ('Class A up until 30 September 2026', employer 9.00 / 11.25), https://www.gov.ie/en/department-of-social-protection/publications/prsi-class-a-rates/, accessed 2026-08-20. Use as context for the scheduled October 2026 step, not as a standalone hook.

entries.title: All PRSI rates rise 0.15 percentage points on 1 October 2026
entries.fact: On 1 October 2026, all PRSI contribution rates increase by 0.15 percentage points, taking employer Class A PRSI from 9% to 9.15% on weekly earnings up to €552 and from 11.25% to 11.4% above €552.

quantification.how: 0.15pp × annual full-time minimum-wage pay (€14.15 × 39h × 52wk = €28,696.20) = €43.04 per employee per year; scales with actual pay

source.quote: From 1 October 2026, employers pay 9.15% Class A employer PRSI on weekly earnings up to €552, or 11.4% if weekly earnings are above €552.

entries.angle: From 1 October 2026 employer PRSI steps up again — 11.4% on most full-time hospitality wages — adding roughly €43 per year per full-time minimum-wage employee, on top of January's 65c minimum wage rise. A dated, stackable number for a Q4 cost-planning opener aimed at Irish multi-site groups.
entries.proof_pairing: Labour-cost visibility proof: a customer that sees fully loaded labour cost (wages + employer PRSI) per site per day and acted on it.
entries.caveats: Verified on both citizensinformation.ie and the gov.ie PRSI Class A rates table ('Class A from 1 October 2026', employer 9.15 / 11.40), https://www.gov.ie/en/department-of-social-protection/publications/prsi-class-a-rates/, accessed 2026-08-20. The per-employee euro figure assumes full-time at minimum wage; it is larger for higher-paid staff. Small number on its own — best stacked with the NMW step and auto-enrolment, not alone. Do not cite steps beyond October 2026 (only published up to that step).

entries.title: Tips and Gratuities Act 2022: display, fair distribution and tip statements
entries.fact: Since 1 December 2022, the Payment of Wages (Amendment) (Tips and Gratuities) Act 2022 requires Irish hospitality employers to prominently display their tips policy, distribute electronic tips fairly, keep tips outside contractual wages, and give each worker a statement showing tips received and their share.

source.quote: Businesses must clearly display their policy on how tips, gratuities and service charges are distributed. ... The employer must provide a statement to workers showing the amount of tips obtained in a period and the portion paid to the individual employee for that particular period.

entries.angle: Every Irish venue taking card tips has, since December 2022, owed each worker a per-period statement of tips received and distributed — a recurring admin task per site per pay period that scales with headcount and site count. Works as a records/admin-burden opener, not a scare line.
entries.proof_pairing: Tronc/tips-handling or payroll-records proof: a customer that automated per-employee tip distribution records across multiple sites.
entries.caveats: Cash tips are not regulated beyond being covered in the displayed policy. The Act required a ministerial review after one year (gov.ie: 'The Act requires the Minister for Enterprise, Trade and Employment to review the legislation after it has been in effect for one year.', https://www.gov.ie/en/department-of-enterprise-tourism-and-employment/publications/payment-of-wages-amendment-tips-and-gratuities-act-2022/, accessed 2026-08-20) and a public consultation was run, but no amending legislation was verified in this session — do not claim changes are coming. Facts only; never advise on how to structure tips or service charges.

entries.title: My Future Fund auto-enrolment: employer contributions from 1 January 2026
entries.fact: Ireland's pension auto-enrolment scheme, My Future Fund, began collecting contributions on 1 January 2026, with employers matching a 1.5% contribution on gross pay for enrolled employees, rising by 1.5 percentage points every three years to 6% by 2035.

quantification.how: 1.5% employer contribution × annual full-time minimum-wage pay (€14.15 × 39h × 52wk = €28,696.20) = €430.44 per enrolled full-time employee per year

source.quote: the collection of contributions for the Automatic Enrolment retirement savings system called My Future Fund will begin from 1st January 2026 ... with both employer and employee contributions starting at 1.5%, and increasing every three years by 1.5% until they eventually reach 6% by Year 10 (2035).

entries.angle: Since 1 January 2026, Irish employers pay a 1.5% My Future Fund contribution on gross pay for auto-enrolled staff — roughly €430 a year per enrolled full-time employee at minimum wage, a brand-new payroll line that did not exist in 2025 and is scheduled to quadruple to 6% by 2035.
entries.proof_pairing: Payroll-integration / labour-cost forecasting proof: a customer whose payroll and forecasting captured a new statutory contribution line without manual rework across sites.
entries.caveats: Only employees aged 23-60 earning over €20,000 across employments and not already in an occupational pension scheme are auto-enrolled, and employees can opt out after six months — so the per-employee figure applies to enrolled staff only, and hospitality's younger/part-time workforce means coverage varies widely by venue. Contribution rate is flat at 1.5% until the first scheduled step-up (every three years); do not present 6% as a near-term cost.
